title: Quantum-interference correction to conductivity in disordered electronic bands with non-uniform quantum geometry
authors: Yip Chun Wong, Asimpunya Mitra, Yong Baek Kim
abstract: Weak localization in two-dimensional disordered electron systems originates from constructive interference between time-reversed scattering paths, giving rise to a logarithmically divergent quantum-interference correction to the dc conductivity. This behavior is generally suppressed when time-reversal symmetry (TRS) is broken. In this study, using a band-projected framework motivated by spin- and valley-polarized rhombohedral $N$-layer graphene (RNG), we show that nonuniform quantum geometry can qualitatively modify quantum-interference corrections to dc transport. In particular, continuously tuning the quantum geometry can change the sign of the conductivity correction, corresponding to a crossover between localization and antilocalization tendencies. Remarkably, at special values of the parameter controlling the quantum geometry, weak-localization (WL) or weak-antilocalization (WAL) can re-emerge despite broken microscopic TRS. At these special points, the orbital structure of the Bloch states gives rise to an emergent antiunitary symmetry that protects a gapless Cooperon mode and restores the logarithmically divergent quantum-interference correction characteristic of WL or WAL. Our results establish nonuniform quantum geometry as a mechanism for controlling quantum interference and electron localization in multiorbital electronic systems.
summary: This theoretical work examines how varying the quantum geometry in disordered electronic bands affects quantum interference corrections to conductivity. By analyzing models based on graphene, the authors show that geometric tuning can induce crossovers between localization and antilocalization. Crucially, they demonstrate that specific geometric points restore gapless Cooperon modes via emergent symmetries, thereby controlling quantum interference effects.
main_problem: The study investigates how non-uniform quantum geometry modifies quantum-interference corrections to DC conductivity in disordered electronic bands, especially when time-reversal symmetry (TRS) is broken.
main_result: Nonuniform quantum geometry can qualitatively change the sign of the conductivity correction, allowing weak-localization or weak-antilocalization to re-emerge at special parameter values by protecting a gapless Cooperon mode via an emergent antiunitary symmetry.
method: The analysis uses a band-projected formalism, employing diagrammatic transport calculations involving the Diffuson and Cooperon propagators derived from solving Bethe-Salpeter equations.
model_or_system: The system is modeled using a band-projected framework, motivated by spin- and valley-polarized rhombohedral N-layer graphene (RNG) and analyzed via the $\lambda$-jellium model.
key_observables: Quantum-interference correction to DC conductivity ($\delta\sigma$), Cooperon mode gap ($\Delta_n$), and the ratio of transport diffusion coefficient to bare diffusion coefficient ($D_{tr}/D_{bare}$).
important_parameters: The dimensionless quantum geometric parameter $ eta = B k_F / 2$, and the number of layers $N$.
main_assumptions: Assumes parabolic dispersion ($\xi_k$) and operates in the weak-disorder regime ($\mu	au \gg 1$).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the quantum-interference correction $\delta\sigma$ vs. $ eta$, showing crossovers between localization and antilocalization. Other figures detail the behavior of $D_{tr}/D_{bare}$ and Berry curvature profiles.
paper_structure: The paper builds from general concepts of quantum interference corrections (Diffuson/Cooperon) to the specific application of the band-projected formalism. It derives the conductivity correction using Hikami boxes, analyzes the role of emergent antiunitary symmetries ($T_N$), and concludes by showing how geometry controls the gap closing and restoration of quantum interference effects.
why_interesting: The concept of emergent symmetries protecting gapless modes in engineered quantum systems is highly relevant to understanding topological phases and robust transport properties, which are key areas in AMO physics and quantum materials.
